skills.chain: A causal chain with every link: the action, the market it hits, the rate, spending, AD, then output and the price level
skills.tool: The right policy tool for the framework named (an administered rate with ample reserves; an open market operation with limited reserves)
skills.graph: The right curve on the right graph, shifted the right way, with the new equilibrium compared with the old
skills.multiplier: The change that closes a gap: the direction first, then the gap divided by the right multiplier
skills.selfadjust: Long-run self-adjustment with its cause: nominal wages and input prices adjust, so SRAS shifts
skills.currency: A currency market read the right way round: the price in units of the other currency, the curve that moves and why
skills.calculate: A calculation with the formula or steps shown, not the answer alone
skills.identify: An explicit statement of the concept, rate or outcome asked for

prompts.title: Scarcity behind a town's choice
prompts.prompt: Merrow's town council can afford a new library or a new park this year, but not both. Explain why the council faces a trade-off, and identify its opportunity cost if it builds the library.
checklist: Names scarcity: the town's resources (its budget, land and workers) are limited
Says choosing one use means giving up the other
Names the park as the opportunity cost of the library

earns.answer: The town's resources are scarce: it has a limited budget, land and workers, so it cannot have every project it wants. Using them on the library means giving them up for the park, so it faces a trade-off, and the opportunity cost of building the library is the park it does not build.
earns.why: It names scarcity as the cause, the trade-off as the result, and the park as the specific opportunity cost.

misses.answer: The council has to choose because it cannot decide what people want.
misses.why: The choice comes from limited resources, not from people's wants being unclear, and no opportunity cost is named.

why.1: Wants are not the limit; resources are.

cost.label: Opportunity cost of the library
options: the budget spent on the library
nothing, if the library is popular

why.1: The budget is the resource used; the cost is the next best thing given up.
why.2: Every choice gives something up, however popular it is.

prompts.title: Opportunity cost from a PPC table
prompts.context:
Production possibilities for Tellis, an invented country:

PointABCD
Tractors0102030
Wheat (tons)90806030
prompts.prompt: Calculate the opportunity cost of each extra tractor when the economy moves from point B to point C, and show your work.
checklist: Finds the wheat given up: 80 - 60 = 20 tons
Finds the tractors gained: 20 - 10 = 10
Divides: 20 / 10 = 2 tons of wheat per tractor

earns.answer: From B to C the economy gives up 80 - 60 = 20 tons of wheat to make 20 - 10 = 10 more tractors. The opportunity cost of each extra tractor is 20 / 10 = 2 tons of wheat.
earns.why: It shows what is given up and what is gained, then divides, with the units.

misses.answer: The opportunity cost is 60 tons of wheat.
misses.why: 60 is the wheat still produced at C, not the wheat given up, and nothing is per tractor.

why.1: 60 tons is what is still made at C; subtract it from 80.
why.2: 80 tons is the amount at B; the cost is the drop.

why.1: That divides tractors by wheat; divide the wheat given up by the tractors gained.
why.2: 20 tons buys all 10 tractors; divide by 10 for one.

prompts.title: Why the PPC bows outward
prompts.prompt: Explain why the opportunity cost of tractors rises as Tellis makes more of them (use the table above if you need numbers).
checklist: States the opportunity cost rises: 1, then 2, then 3 tons of wheat per tractor
Explains that resources are not equally good at making both goods
Links the rising cost to the bowed-out shape of the PPC

earns.answer: Each block of 10 tractors costs more wheat: 10 tons, then 20, then 30, so 1, 2, then 3 tons per tractor. Resources are not equally suited to both goods, so the first tractors use the workers and land least useful for wheat, and later ones pull in resources that are very good at farming. That rising opportunity cost is why the PPC bows outward.
earns.why: It shows the cost rising with numbers and explains why: resources are specialized.

misses.answer: Tractors get more expensive because people want more of them.
misses.why: Demand plays no part in a PPC; the cause is that resources are not equally good at both goods.

trend.label: As tractors rise, their opportunity cost

why.1: Each block of tractors gives up more wheat than the last, so the cost rises.
why.2: A constant cost would give a straight-line PPC.

why.label: Because
options: resources are not equally suited to both goods
tractors need more workers than wheat

why.1: What matters is how well resources switch between goods, not how many workers a good needs.

prompts.title: A point inside the PPC
prompts.prompt: During a slump, many of Tellis's workers and machines sit idle. Explain where its output is shown on a correctly labeled PPC, and describe how it could produce more of both goods.
checklist: Places output at a point inside the PPC
Says resources sit idle, so production is not efficient
Says putting idle resources to work moves the point toward the curve, more of both goods

earns.answer: With workers and machines idle, Tellis produces at a point inside its PPC (tractors on one axis, wheat on the other). It is not using all its resources, so it is not productively efficient. Putting the idle resources back to work moves the point out toward the curve, so it can make more tractors and more wheat with no trade-off.
earns.why: It places the point correctly, says why, and explains how more of both is possible.

misses.answer: The PPC shifts inward because workers lose their jobs.
misses.why: Idle resources still exist, so the curve does not move; output sits at a point inside it.

why.1: On the curve means every resource is used; here many are idle.
why.2: Outside the curve is unattainable with today's resources.

why.1: The resources still exist; idling them moves the point, not the curve.

prompts.title: Finding comparative advantage
prompts.context:
Output per worker per week in two invented countries:

CountryCloth (bolts)Wheat (tons)
Dellow63
Varro44
prompts.prompt: Determine which country has the comparative advantage in wheat, and show the opportunity costs that support your answer.
checklist: Finds Dellow's opportunity cost of 1 ton of wheat: 6 / 3 = 2 bolts of cloth
Finds Varro's opportunity cost of 1 ton of wheat: 4 / 4 = 1 bolt of cloth
Gives Varro the comparative advantage in wheat because its opportunity cost is lower

earns.answer: In Dellow a worker gives up 6 / 3 = 2 bolts of cloth for each ton of wheat; in Varro, 4 / 4 = 1 bolt. Varro gives up less cloth for each ton of wheat, so Varro has the comparative advantage in wheat (and Dellow in cloth).
earns.why: It computes both opportunity costs and picks the lower one, which is what comparative advantage means.

misses.answer: Dellow has the comparative advantage in wheat, because its workers make more cloth.
misses.why: Making more cloth is an absolute advantage in cloth; comparative advantage in wheat goes to the lower opportunity cost of wheat.

dellow.label: Dellow's cost of a ton of wheat

why.1: That is cloth's cost in wheat; divide cloth by wheat for wheat's cost.
why.2: 3 is Dellow's wheat output, not a cost.

why.1: Dellow gives up 2 bolts per ton, more than Varro's 1.

prompts.title: Terms of trade that help both
prompts.prompt: Dellow and Varro (above) agree to trade 1 ton of wheat for 1.5 bolts of cloth. Explain why both countries gain from these terms of trade.
checklist: States Varro gets 1.5 bolts per ton, more than its own cost of 1 bolt
States Dellow pays 1.5 bolts per ton, less than its own cost of 2 bolts
Concludes the terms lie between the two opportunity costs, so both gain

earns.answer: Varro gives up 1 bolt of cloth to make a ton of wheat but gets 1.5 bolts for it in trade, so it gains. Dellow would give up 2 bolts to make a ton of wheat itself but gets one for 1.5 bolts, so it gains too. The terms of trade lie between the two opportunity costs, which is why both are better off.
earns.why: It compares the terms with each country's own opportunity cost, so the gain for each side is shown.

misses.answer: Both countries gain because trade between countries is good for everyone.
misses.why: There is no comparison with either country's opportunity cost, so nothing shows that these terms help both.

varro.label: Varro gets per ton of wheat
options: more cloth than it gives up at home
less cloth than it gives up at home

why.1: 1.5 bolts is more than Varro's own cost of 1 bolt.
Below 1 bolt, Varro would do better making cloth itself.
why.2: Above 2 bolts, Dellow would do better making wheat itself.

prompts.title: A price change is a movement along demand
prompts.prompt: The price of movie tickets rises. Explain what happens on a correctly labeled graph of the market for movie tickets, using the right terms.
checklist: Says the change is a movement along the demand curve, not a shift
Says the quantity demanded falls (not demand)
Explains why: the good's own price is on the vertical axis

earns.answer: The ticket price is on the vertical axis, so a rise in it is a movement up along the demand curve, not a shift. The quantity demanded falls, while demand (the whole curve) stays the same.
earns.why: It uses "quantity demanded" and "movement along" correctly and gives the reason.

misses.answer: Demand for movie tickets decreases, so the demand curve shifts left.
misses.why: A change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve; it changes the quantity demanded along the curve.

what.label: On the graph
options: a movement along the demand curve

why.1: The good's own price is on an axis, so its change moves along the curve.
"Demand" is the whole curve, which does not move here.

prompts.title: An input price shifts supply
prompts.prompt: The price of flour rises. Explain the effect on the market for bread, and identify what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity.
checklist: Says flour is an input, so the supply of bread shifts left
Says the demand for bread does not shift
States the equilibrium price rises and the equilibrium quantity falls

earns.answer: Flour is an input to bread, so a higher flour price raises bakers' costs at every price and shifts the supply of bread left. Demand does not change. At the new equilibrium the price of bread is higher and the quantity bought and sold is lower.
earns.why: It names the curve that moves, why, which way, and both equilibrium changes.

misses.answer: The price of bread rises, so people buy less bread.
misses.why: It skips the cause and the curve: nothing says supply shifts left because flour is an input.

why.1: Buyers' wants did not change; bakers' costs did.
why.2: Higher costs mean less is supplied at each price.

why.1: Less supply at each price leaves a shortage at the old price, so the price rises.

prompts.title: A price below equilibrium
prompts.prompt: In a market for concert tickets, the price is set below the equilibrium price. Explain what the market shows at this price and what would bring it back to equilibrium.
checklist: Says the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied
Names the gap between them a shortage
Explains that the price would rise, lowering quantity demanded and raising quantity supplied until they are equal

earns.answer: Below the equilibrium price, the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Buyers compete for the few tickets, which pushes the price up; as it rises the quantity demanded falls and the quantity supplied rises until they are equal at equilibrium.
earns.why: It names the shortage with its cause and gives the path back to equilibrium on both sides of the market.

misses.answer: There is a surplus, because the price is too low for sellers.
misses.why: A low price leaves buyers wanting more than sellers offer, which is a shortage, not a surplus.

why.1: A surplus happens above equilibrium, when sellers offer more than buyers want.
A lower price would make the shortage bigger.
why.2: The curves do not move; the price moves along them.

prompts.title: Both curves shift at once
prompts.prompt: A new study praises oat milk, and at the same time new factories cut the cost of making it. Explain the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity of oat milk.
checklist: Says demand shifts right and supply shifts right
States the equilibrium quantity rises
States the change in price is indeterminate without the sizes of the shifts

earns.answer: The study shifts demand right, and lower costs shift supply right. Both shifts raise the equilibrium quantity. Demand pushes the price up while supply pushes it down, so the change in price is indeterminate unless we know which shift is larger.
earns.why: It names both shifts, gives the one determinate result, and says why the other cannot be signed.

misses.answer: The price and quantity of oat milk both rise.
misses.why: The rise in supply pulls the price down, so a rise in price is not certain; the answer leaves out supply.

why.1: Both shifts push the quantity up.
why.2: Both shifts move quantity the same way, so it can be signed.

why.1: Supply's rise pulls the price down, so a rise is not certain.
why.2: Demand's rise pulls the price up, so a fall is not certain.

prompts.title: GDP from spending
prompts.context:
Corlin, an invented country, billions of dollars in one year:

Consumption600
Investment150
Government purchases of goods and services200
Exports80
Imports100
Transfer payments50
prompts.prompt: Calculate Corlin's GDP, and explain why one item in the table is left out.
checklist: Gets a GDP of 930 billion dollars for the year
Leaves out transfer payments because they buy no new good or service

earns.answer: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M) = 600 + 150 + 200 + (80 - 100) = 930 billion dollars. Transfer payments (50 billion) are left out: they move income from taxpayers to recipients but pay for no new good or service.
earns.why: It writes the formula with the values, gets the total, and gives the reason for the item left out.

misses.answer: GDP is 600 + 150 + 200 + 80 + 100 + 50 = 1,180 billion dollars.
misses.why: Imports are subtracted, not added, and transfer payments are not purchases of output.

why.1: Imports are made abroad, so they are taken out of spending on domestic output.
Transfers buy no good or service, so they are not part of government purchases.

prompts.title: What GDP counts
prompts.prompt: This year Ada buys a used car for $8,000 and shares in a company for $2,000. Explain how each purchase affects this year's GDP.
checklist: Says the used car adds nothing: it was produced and counted in an earlier year
Says the shares add nothing: they are a transfer of ownership, not new output
Adds that a dealer's fee for the sale would count, as a service produced this year

earns.answer: Neither purchase adds to this year's GDP. The used car was counted in the year it was made, so selling it again is not new production. Shares in a company pass ownership of a company from one person to another; no good or service is produced. Only a fee paid this year to a dealer or broker for the sale would count, as a service produced now.
earns.why: It gives the reason for each purchase in terms of new final production and notes what would count.

misses.answer: Both add to GDP, $10,000 in all, because Ada paid for them this year.
misses.why: Spending is counted only when it buys new final goods and services; a used car and company shares are neither.

why.1: It was counted when it was produced, so counting it again would double count.
In GDP, investment means new capital goods, not shares in a company.

prompts.title: GDP per capita and well-being
prompts.prompt: Country L's GDP grows 2% a year while its population grows 3% a year. Explain what happens to GDP per capita, and identify one thing GDP per capita still leaves out about well-being.
checklist: States GDP per capita falls, because population grows faster than GDP
Names one thing left out, such as leisure, pollution, nonmarket work or how income is shared
Links that item to why GDP per capita is an imperfect measure

earns.answer: GDP per capita is GDP divided by population. Population is growing faster than GDP, so GDP per capita falls, even though total GDP grows. It still leaves out nonmarket activity, such as care given at home, so it understates what people produce and enjoy.
earns.why: It reasons from the two growth rates to the per-person result and names a specific limitation with its effect.

misses.answer: GDP per capita rises because GDP is growing.
misses.why: Total GDP grows, but more slowly than the population, so the amount per person falls; no limitation is named.

why.1: Population grows by more than GDP, so each person's share shrinks.
why.2: The two growth rates differ, so the ratio changes.

why.1: New houses are counted, as investment.

prompts.title: Unemployment and participation rates
prompts.context:
Sennet, an invented country, millions of people:

Adult population300
Employed190
Unemployed10
prompts.prompt: Calculate Sennet's unemployment rate and its labor force participation rate, and show your work.
checklist: Finds the labor force: 190 + 10 = 200 million
Unemployment rate: 10 / 200 x 100 = 5%
Participation rate: 200 / 300 x 100, about 66.7%

earns.answer: The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed: 190 + 10 = 200 million. The unemployment rate is 10 / 200 x 100 = 5%. The participation rate is the labor force divided by the adult population: 200 / 300 x 100, about 66.7%.
earns.why: Each rate has its formula with the right denominator and the values filled in.

misses.answer: The unemployment rate is 10 / 300, about 3.3%, and participation is 190 / 300.
misses.why: The unemployment rate divides by the labor force, not the adult population, and the labor force includes the unemployed.

why.1: The unemployed are part of the labor force too.
why.2: 300 million is the adult population, which includes people not in the labor force.

why.1: That divides by adults; divide by the labor force.
why.2: That divides by the employed; divide by the labor force.

prompts.title: Natural and cyclical unemployment
prompts.prompt: Halvet's unemployment rate is 7%. Frictional unemployment is 2% and structural unemployment is 3%. Calculate the natural rate and cyclical unemployment, and explain what the cyclical rate tells you.
checklist: Natural rate = frictional + structural = 2% + 3% = 5%
Cyclical = actual - natural = 7% - 5% = 2%
Says positive cyclical unemployment means output is below potential: a downturn

earns.answer: The natural rate is frictional plus structural: 2% + 3% = 5%. Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate: 7% - 5% = 2%. A positive cyclical rate means the economy is producing below its potential output, as in a contraction.
earns.why: Both formulas are written with values, and the meaning of the cyclical rate is stated.

misses.answer: The natural rate is 7%, because that is the unemployment rate.
misses.why: The natural rate leaves out cyclical unemployment; it is frictional plus structural, 5%.

why.1: 7% is the actual rate, which includes cyclical unemployment.
why.2: That adds the actual rate too; the natural rate is frictional plus structural.

why.1: That subtracts structural alone; subtract the whole natural rate.

prompts.title: Naming a type of unemployment
prompts.prompt: Pia ran a printing press for 15 years. Her plant switched to digital machines, and the jobs near her need computer skills she does not have. She is looking for work. Identify the type of unemployment and explain your answer.
checklist: Names structural unemployment
Explains her skills no longer match the jobs available
Says it is not cyclical: the cause is a change in technology, not a downturn

earns.answer: Pia is structurally unemployed. The jobs open near her need skills she lacks, because technology changed what her industry needs; her skills no longer match the jobs. It is not cyclical, since the cause is not a fall in overall spending but a change in technology.
earns.why: It names the type, ties it to the skills mismatch, and rules out the near miss.

misses.answer: Pia is cyclically unemployed, because she lost her job.
misses.why: Losing a job does not make unemployment cyclical; here the cause is a mismatch of skills after a change in technology.

why.1: Cyclical unemployment comes from a downturn in the whole economy.
why.2: Frictional unemployment is the time it takes to find a job one has the skills for.

why.label: Because
options: her skills do not match the jobs available
the economy is in a contraction

why.1: Nothing says the economy is in a downturn; her skills are the problem.

prompts.title: A price index and the inflation rate
prompts.prompt: A basket of goods cost $250 in the base year and $270 a year later. Calculate the CPI for the later year and the inflation rate between the two years.
checklist: Inflation rate = (108 - 100) / 100 x 100 = 8%
Notes the base year's CPI is 100

earns.answer: The CPI is the basket's cost now over its cost in the base year, times 100: 270 / 250 x 100 = 108. The base year is 100, so the inflation rate is (108 - 100) / 100 x 100 = 8%.
earns.why: The index and the rate each come with their formula and values.

misses.answer: Prices went up by $20, so inflation is 20%.
misses.why: Inflation is the percent change in the index, (108 - 100) / 100, not the dollar change in the basket.

why.1: That divides the base-year cost by the later cost; flip it.
why.2: 20 is the change in dollars, not an index.

why.1: Divide the change by the starting value.
why.2: 108 is the index level, not its change.

prompts.title: Who loses from surprise inflation
prompts.prompt: Joss lent his sister $1,000 for a year at a fixed 3%, expecting prices to be stable. Inflation turns out to be 6%. Explain who gains and who loses from the inflation.
checklist: Says Joss (the lender) loses: the dollars repaid buy less than he expected
Says his sister (the borrower) gains: she repays in dollars worth less
Ties the effect to the inflation being unanticipated

earns.answer: The inflation was not anticipated, so the fixed 3% did not cover it. Joss is repaid $1,030, but prices rose 6%, so those dollars buy less than the $1,000 he lent: the lender loses. His sister gains, because she repays in dollars that are worth less than when she borrowed.
earns.why: It names both sides, explains with buying power, and ties it to the inflation being unexpected.

misses.answer: Everyone loses from inflation because prices are higher.
misses.why: Unanticipated inflation moves buying power from lenders to borrowers; the borrower here gains.

why.1: The dollars he gets back buy less than he expected.
She repays in dollars worth less, which helps her.

prompts.title: Real GDP from the deflator
prompts.prompt: Riven's nominal GDP is 1,320 billion dollars and its GDP deflator is 110. Calculate real GDP, and explain what the deflator says about prices compared with the base year.
checklist: Real GDP = nominal / deflator x 100 = 1,320 / 110 x 100
Gets 1,200 billion dollars
Says prices are 10% higher than in the base year

earns.answer: Real GDP = nominal GDP / deflator x 100 = 1,320 / 110 x 100 = 1,200 billion dollars. A deflator of 110 means prices are on average 10% higher than in the base year, so real GDP is smaller than nominal GDP.
earns.why: It divides by the deflator (not multiplies), shows the values, and reads the deflator correctly.

misses.answer: Real GDP is 1,320 x 1.1 = 1,452 billion dollars.
misses.why: That multiplies by the deflator; removing price increases means dividing by it.

op.label: To remove price changes
options: divide by the deflator and multiply by 100

why.1: Multiplying adds the price rise again; divide to take it out.
That multiplies by 1.1.
why.2: That subtracts 110 from nominal GDP.

prompts.title: An output gap
prompts.prompt: Bracken's potential output is 900 billion dollars, and its real GDP this year is 860 billion dollars. Identify the output gap and explain what it implies for unemployment.
checklist: Finds real GDP is 40 billion dollars below potential output
Calls it a negative output gap
Says unemployment is above the natural rate: cyclical unemployment is positive

earns.answer: Real GDP is 860, which is 900 - 860 = 40 billion dollars below potential output: a negative output gap. The economy is not using all its resources, so unemployment is above the natural rate and cyclical unemployment is positive.
earns.why: It sizes the gap, names its sign, and links it to unemployment.

misses.answer: The economy is 860 billion dollars, so it is in a boom.
misses.why: Real GDP below potential means a negative gap and high unemployment, not a boom.

why.1: Real GDP is below potential, so the gap is negative.
Output below potential means idle workers, so unemployment is above the natural rate.

prompts.title: Why aggregate demand slopes down
prompts.prompt: Explain why a fall in the price level raises the quantity of real output demanded, using the wealth effect.
checklist: Says a lower price level raises the buying power of people's savings (real wealth)
Says higher real wealth raises consumption
Calls it a movement along AD, not a shift

earns.answer: When the price level falls, the savings people hold buy more, so their real wealth rises. Feeling wealthier, households consume more, so the quantity of real output demanded rises. This is a movement down along the AD curve, not a shift of it.
earns.why: It names the mechanism step by step and keeps it a movement along the curve.

misses.answer: When prices fall, people buy more, like on a demand curve for one good.
misses.why: AD is not a single good's demand: the reason has to be a whole-economy effect such as the wealth effect, and it is not named.

wealth.label: A lower price level makes real wealth

why.1: The same savings buy more at lower prices, so real wealth rises.
The price level is on an axis, so its change moves along AD.

prompts.title: A fall in confidence, link by link
prompts.prompt: Households in Quell become worried about their jobs. Explain the effect on real output and the price level in the short run, naming every link.
checklist: Says worried households cut consumption
Says lower consumption shifts AD left
Says real output falls and the price level falls, so unemployment rises

earns.answer: Worried households save more and cut consumption, which lowers aggregate demand, so AD shifts left. With AD lower, firms sell less, so real output falls and the price level falls, which raises unemployment.
earns.why: Every link from the worry to output and prices is there, in order.

misses.answer: People are worried, so real output falls.
misses.why: It jumps from the cause to the result; consumption and AD, the links between them, are missing.

why.1: Worried households spend less and save more.

ad.label: Then AD
options: does not move, as only SRAS changes

why.1: Less consumption at every price level lowers AD.
why.2: Consumption is part of AD, so AD moves.

why.1: A leftward AD shift lowers the price level along SRAS.

prompts.title: The largest change from new investment
prompts.prompt: In Corvane the MPC is 0.9. Firms raise investment by 20 billion dollars. Calculate the spending multiplier and the largest possible change in real GDP.
checklist: Multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.1 = 10
Change in real GDP = 20 x 10 = 200 billion dollars
Says it is an increase, the most it can be with no price changes

earns.answer: The spending multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 1 / 0.1 = 10. The largest possible change in real GDP is 20 x 10 = 200 billion dollars, an increase, because each round of spending becomes someone's income and part of it is spent again.
earns.why: The multiplier formula and the product are both shown, with the direction.

misses.answer: Real GDP rises by 20 / 0.9, about 22 billion dollars.
misses.why: The multiplier is 1 over the MPS, not over the MPC, and the investment is multiplied, not divided.

why.1: That is 1 divided by the MPC; use 1 divided by the MPS.
why.2: That is MPC divided by MPS, the size of the tax multiplier.

dy.label: The largest change in real GDP

why.1: The first round alone; rounds of spending add more.
why.2: That divides the investment by the multiplier.

prompts.title: Higher nominal wages on the AD-AS graph
prompts.prompt: Workers across Fendle win higher nominal wages. Explain the effect on a correctly labeled AD-AS graph, and identify the changes in the price level and real output.
checklist: Says SRAS shifts left, because wage costs rise at every price level
Says AD does not shift, since spending plans are unchanged
States the price level rises and real output falls (cost-push inflation)

earns.answer: Higher nominal wages raise firms' costs at every price level, so SRAS shifts left (SRAS1 to SRAS2), while AD stays put. The new short-run equilibrium has a higher price level and lower real output: cost-push inflation.
earns.why: Right curve, right direction, the reason, and both outcomes against the old equilibrium.

misses.answer: Higher wages give workers more to spend, so AD shifts right and real output rises.
misses.why: Wage costs are what a nationwide wage rise changes first; the answer shifts AD instead of SRAS.

why.1: Wages are a cost of production, so supply moves.
why.2: LRAS depends on resources and technology, not on wages.

why.1: A leftward SRAS shift lowers output along AD.

prompts.title: Why LRAS is vertical
prompts.prompt: Explain why the long-run aggregate supply curve is vertical at full-employment output.
checklist: Says in the long run wages and other input prices fully adjust to the price level
Says output then depends on resources and technology, not on the price level
Places LRAS at full-employment output (YF)

earns.answer: In the long run, nominal wages and other input prices adjust fully to the price level, so a higher price level no longer makes production more profitable. Output then depends on the economy's resources and technology, so it is the same at any price level: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, YF.
earns.why: It gives the long-run adjustment of input prices and what sets output instead.

misses.answer: LRAS is vertical because the economy is at its maximum output.
misses.why: Full employment is not the most an economy can ever produce, and no reason is given for output not depending on the price level.

why.label: In the long run
options: input prices adjust to the price level

why.1: Prices can still change; what matters is that wages catch up with them.
Output can exceed YF for a while, so YF is not a maximum.

prompts.title: Out of a recessionary gap with no policy
prompts.prompt: Lanmore is in a recessionary gap, and the government does nothing. Explain how the economy returns to full employment in the long run, and identify the change in the price level.
checklist: Says unemployment above the natural rate puts downward pressure on nominal wages
Says lower wages and input prices shift SRAS right
Says output returns to full employment at a lower price level

earns.answer: With output below full employment, unemployment is above the natural rate, so over time nominal wages and other input prices fall. Lower costs shift SRAS right, which raises real output back to full employment, where SRAS meets AD on LRAS, at a lower price level.
earns.why: It gives the cause (falling wages), the curve (SRAS shifts right) and both results.

misses.answer: The economy recovers on its own as AD rises back to normal.
misses.why: Self-adjustment works through wages and SRAS; nothing here makes AD rise.

why.1: High unemployment pushes wages down, not up.
No policy or spending change moves AD.
why.2: LRAS does not move to meet the economy.

why.1: SRAS shifting right lowers the price level along AD.

prompts.title: Out of an inflationary gap with no policy
prompts.prompt: Lanmore later has an inflationary gap, and again there is no policy. Explain the long-run adjustment and its effect on the price level.
checklist: Says unemployment below the natural rate pushes nominal wages up
Says higher wages shift SRAS left
Says output returns to full employment at a higher price level

earns.answer: Output is above full employment, so unemployment is below the natural rate and workers win higher nominal wages. Higher costs shift SRAS left, which lowers real output back to full employment at a higher price level.
earns.why: It names the wage cause, the SRAS shift and both outcomes.

misses.answer: Prices rise until people buy less, so output falls back to full employment.
misses.why: It describes a movement along AD with no cause; the adjustment is rising wages shifting SRAS left.

why.1: A tight labor market pushes wages up.
Higher costs lower what firms supply at each price level.

prompts.title: Closing a gap with government purchases
prompts.prompt: Orvel has a recessionary gap of 120 billion dollars and an MPC of 0.75. Calculate the smallest change in government purchases that closes the gap, and show your work.
checklist: Says purchases must rise, because the gap is recessionary
Finds the multiplier: 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4
Divides the gap by the multiplier: 120 / 4 = 30 billion dollars

earns.answer: The gap is recessionary, so purchases must rise. The spending multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.75) = 4, so the change needed is the gap divided by the multiplier: 120 / 4 = an increase of 30 billion dollars.
earns.why: Direction first, then the gap divided by the right multiplier, with the work shown.

misses.answer: Government purchases should rise by 120 x 4 = 480 billion dollars.
misses.why: That multiplies the gap; the multiplier turns the change into the gap, so the change is the gap divided by it.

why.1: A recessionary gap needs more spending.
Multiplying by 4 gives 480, sixteen times the change that closes the gap.
That multiplies by 4.
why.2: That is the whole gap; the multiplier makes up the rest.

prompts.title: Closing the same gap with a tax cut
prompts.prompt: Orvel (above) uses a tax cut instead. Calculate the tax cut that closes the 120 billion dollar recessionary gap with an MPC of 0.75, and explain why it is larger than the change in purchases.
checklist: Finds the tax multiplier: 0.75 / 0.25 = 3 (in size)
Divides the gap by it: 120 / 3 = a tax cut of 40 billion dollars
Explains households save part of a tax cut before spending it, so the first round is smaller

earns.answer: The tax multiplier is MPC / MPS = 0.75 / 0.25 = 3 in size. The tax cut that closes the gap is the gap divided by it: 120 / 3 = 40 billion dollars. It is larger than the 30 billion change in purchases because households save a quarter of a tax cut before spending the rest.
earns.why: It uses the tax multiplier, divides, and explains the difference from purchases.

misses.answer: Cut taxes by 30 billion dollars, the same as the change in purchases.
misses.why: A tax cut has a smaller multiplier (3, not 4), so it must be larger to close the same gap.

why.1: 4 is the spending multiplier.
why.2: That is the MPC; the tax multiplier is MPC / MPS.

why.1: That uses the spending multiplier.
why.2: That multiplies the gap by 3.

prompts.title: How an income tax cushions a downturn
prompts.prompt: Real output falls in Pradin, which has a progressive income tax and unemployment benefits. Explain how these automatically soften the fall in output, naming every link.
checklist: Says incomes fall, so tax collections fall and benefit payments rise
Says disposable income falls by less than income
Says consumption falls by less, so AD falls by less and output falls less

earns.answer: As output and incomes fall, people pay less income tax and more people receive unemployment benefits, so disposable income falls by less than income. Consumption then falls by less, which means AD shifts left by less, so real output falls less than it would without them.
earns.why: Every link from lower income to a smaller fall in output is named.

misses.answer: The tax and benefits help the economy in a recession.
misses.why: It gives no mechanism: nothing says taxes fall, benefits rise, or how that keeps consumption and AD up.

why.1: Lower incomes mean less income tax is owed.
Lower taxes and more benefits cushion the fall.
The stabilizers soften the fall in AD; they do not reverse it.

prompts.title: Bond prices when interest rates rise
prompts.prompt: Talia owns a bond that pays 3% a year. New bonds now pay 5%. Explain what happens to the price of Talia's bond.
checklist: Says new bonds pay more, so buyers prefer them
Says Talia's bond must sell at a lower price to attract a buyer
States the rule: bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions

earns.answer: Buyers can now get 5% on a new bond, so no one will pay full price for a bond paying 3%. Talia's bond has to sell at a lower price, so its price falls. Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions.
earns.why: It explains the mechanism with the two rates and states the inverse relationship.

misses.answer: Her bond is worth more because interest rates are higher now.
misses.why: A higher market rate makes an old, lower-paying bond less attractive, so its price falls.

why.1: The new bonds pay more each year for the same price.
It pays less than new bonds, so it must cost less.
why.2: Its fixed payment is worth less when new bonds pay more.

prompts.title: Expected and actual real interest rates
prompts.prompt: Ressa's bank lends at a nominal interest rate of 8%, expecting inflation of 3%. Inflation turns out to be 6%. Calculate the real rate the bank expected and the real rate it earned, and explain who gains.
checklist: Expected real rate = 8% - 3% = 5%
Real rate earned = 8% - 6% = 2%
Says the borrower gains and the bank loses from the surprise inflation

earns.answer: The bank expected a real interest rate of 8% - 3% = 5%. With actual inflation of 6%, it earned 8% - 6% = 2%. The unexpected inflation moves buying power to the borrower, who gains, while the bank loses.
earns.why: Both real rates are computed from the right inflation figure, and the winner is named.

misses.answer: The real rate the bank earns is 8% + 6% = 14% for the year.
misses.why: The real rate subtracts inflation from the nominal rate; adding it goes the wrong way.

why.1: That adds expected inflation.
why.2: That uses the actual inflation, not the expected.

why.1: That is the rate the bank expected; inflation came in higher.

prompts.title: The three functions of money
prompts.prompt: Identify the function of money in each case and explain one: (1) a menu lists every meal's price in dollars; (2) Kim pays for groceries with her debit card; (3) Sam keeps $300 in his checking account for a trip next month.
checklist: (1) unit of account: prices are measured in money
(2) medium of exchange: money is accepted in trade
(3) store of value: money holds buying power until later

earns.answer: (1) The menu uses money as a unit of account, a common measure of value. (2) Paying for groceries uses money as a medium of exchange. (3) Keeping $300 for next month uses money as a store of value: it holds buying power over time, without having to find a buyer for some other good later.
earns.why: Each case gets the right function, and the explanation says what the function does.

misses.answer: All three are money being used to buy things.
misses.why: Only the second is a purchase; pricing and saving are the other two functions, and none is named.

why.2: Nothing is being saved; the menu measures value.

prompts.title: A new deposit and the money supply
prompts.prompt: Under limited reserves with a required reserve ratio of 0.1, Rafe deposits $1,000 of cash in his checking account. Calculate the bank's new excess reserves and the largest possible change in the money supply from the bank lending them.
checklist: Required reserves: 1,000 x 0.1 = $100; excess reserves: 1,000 - 100 = $900
Money multiplier: 1 / 0.1 = 10
Largest change from lending: 900 x 10 = $9,000

earns.answer: Required reserves on the deposit are 1,000 x 0.1 = $100, so excess reserves are 1,000 - 100 = $900. The money multiplier is 1 / 0.1 = 10, so lending the excess reserves can raise the money supply by at most 900 x 10 = $9,000. The deposit itself does not change the money supply, since cash became a checkable deposit.
earns.why: It finds excess reserves first and multiplies those, not the whole deposit, with every step shown.

misses.answer: The money supply can rise by 1,000 x 10 = $10,000.

prompts.title: A bond purchase on the money market graph
prompts.prompt: Danby's central bank, which works with limited reserves, buys government bonds. Explain the effect on a correctly labeled money market graph.
checklist: Labels the axes: nominal interest rate and quantity of money
Says buying bonds adds bank reserves, so the money supply (vertical) shifts right
Says the nominal interest rate falls from i1 to i2

earns.answer: On a money market graph (nominal interest rate on the vertical axis, quantity of money on the horizontal), buying bonds pays money into banks' reserves, so banks can lend more and the money supply rises: MS shifts right from MS1 to MS2. With money demand unchanged, the nominal interest rate falls from i1 to i2.
earns.why: Correct axes, the right curve and direction, and the new rate compared with the old.

misses.answer: The real interest rate falls because money demand shifts right.
misses.why: The money market uses the nominal rate, and the curve that moves is the money supply, not money demand.

why.1: The money market uses the nominal rate; the real rate is for loanable funds.
The central bank's purchase changes the quantity of money, not how much people want to hold.
why.2: Buying bonds adds money; selling would remove it.

prompts.title: A higher price level and money demand
prompts.prompt: The price level in Danby rises, and the central bank does not act. Explain the effect on the money market and the nominal interest rate.
checklist: Says people need more money for the same purchases, so money demand shifts right
Says the money supply does not move
Says the nominal interest rate rises

earns.answer: With a higher price level, people need more money to buy the same goods, so money demand shifts right from MD1 to MD2. The money supply does not move, so the nominal interest rate rises from i1 to i2.
earns.why: It names the curve that moves and why, and compares the new rate with the old.

misses.answer: The money supply falls, so the interest rate rises.
misses.why: Nothing changed the money supply; the higher price level raises money demand.

why.1: The central bank did not act, so the money supply is unchanged.
More demand for a fixed money supply raises its price, the interest rate.

prompts.title: The tool for a recession with ample reserves
prompts.prompt: Pellow's central bank operates with ample reserves, and the economy is in a recession. Identify the action the central bank would take and explain how it changes the policy rate.
checklist: Names lowering its administered rates, such as the interest rate on reserve balances
Says reserve supply is not changed to move the rate
Says the policy rate falls with the administered rate

earns.answer: With ample reserves, the central bank lowers its administered rates, chiefly the interest rate on reserve balances. Banks earn less for holding reserves, so the rate at which they lend reserves to each other, the policy rate, falls with it. The supply of reserves is not changed to move the rate.
earns.why: The tool matches the framework, and the link to the policy rate is explained.

misses.answer: The central bank buys bonds to increase the money supply.
misses.why: Buying bonds is the limited-reserves tool; with ample reserves the rate is moved by the administered rates.

tool.label: The tool
options: lower the interest rate on reserve balances

why.1: Open market operations set the rate in a limited-reserves framework.
why.2: Reserve requirements play no part with ample reserves.

prompts.title: The tool for inflation with limited reserves
prompts.prompt: Corra's central bank works with limited reserves, and the economy has an inflationary gap. Identify an open market operation it would use and explain its effect on the money supply and the nominal interest rate.
checklist: Names selling government bonds
Says buyers pay with money that leaves bank reserves, so the money supply falls
Says the nominal interest rate rises

earns.answer: The central bank sells government bonds. Buyers pay for them with money that leaves banks' reserves, so banks lend less and the money supply falls (MS shifts left). With money demand unchanged, the nominal interest rate rises, which lowers investment and AD to close the gap.
earns.why: The open market operation fits the gap, and its effect on reserves, the money supply and the rate is explained.

misses.answer: The central bank raises taxes to slow spending.
misses.why: Taxes are fiscal policy, set by the government, not a central bank tool.

why.1: Buying bonds adds reserves, which raises the money supply.
Money paid for the bonds leaves the banking system.

prompts.title: From a lower policy rate to real output
prompts.prompt: Pellow's central bank (above) lowers the interest rate on reserve balances. Explain how this affects real output and the price level in the short run, naming every link.
checklist: Says the policy rate falls, and other interest rates follow
Says lower rates raise investment and interest-sensitive consumption
Says AD shifts right, so real output and the price level rise

earns.answer: The lower administered rate lowers the policy rate, which lowers other interest rates in the economy. Cheaper borrowing raises investment and interest-sensitive consumption, which shifts AD right, so real output rises and the price level rises in the short run.
earns.why: Every link from the tool to output and prices is named in order.

misses.answer: Lower interest rates raise real output and the price level.
misses.why: The links between the rate and output, spending and AD, are missing.

why.1: Banks pass the lower policy rate on to borrowers.
Cheaper borrowing makes more projects worth doing.
Spending changed, so demand moves, not supply.

prompts.title: More saving in the loanable funds market
prompts.prompt: Households in Fenwick decide to save a larger share of their income. Explain the effect on a correctly labeled loanable funds graph.
checklist: Labels the axes: real interest rate and quantity of loanable funds
Says the supply of loanable funds shifts right
Says the real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises

earns.answer: On the loanable funds graph (real interest rate on the vertical axis, quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal), more saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, from SLF1 to SLF2. The real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds borrowed and lent rises.
earns.why: Correct axes, the right curve and direction, and both outcomes compared with the start.

misses.answer: The nominal interest rate falls because the demand for loanable funds rises.
misses.why: Saving is the supply of loanable funds, and that market uses the real interest rate.

why.1: Savers supply loanable funds; borrowers demand them.
More funds to lend at each rate lower the rate.

prompts.title: Two expansionary policies at once
prompts.prompt: Sundra's legislature cuts income taxes while its central bank, with ample reserves, lowers the interest rate on reserve balances. Explain the effect on aggregate demand and on interest rates in the short run.
checklist: Says both policies raise AD, so AD rises for sure
Says the tax cut pushes interest rates up while the lower administered rate pushes them down
Concludes the change in interest rates is indeterminate without the sizes

earns.answer: Both policies are expansionary: the tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, and the lower administered rate lowers borrowing costs, so AD rises for sure. But the tax cut raises the demand for money and borrowing, which pushes interest rates up, while the central bank's action pushes them down, so the change in interest rates is indeterminate without their sizes.
earns.why: It signs the variable both policies move the same way and explains why the other cannot be signed.

misses.answer: Aggregate demand rises, and interest rates in Sundra fall for sure.
misses.why: The fall in rates is not certain: the tax cut pushes rates up, so without sizes the change is indeterminate.

why.1: Both policies push AD the same way, so its change can be signed.
The tax cut pushes rates up, so a fall is not certain.
why.2: The central bank pushes rates down, so a rise is not certain.

prompts.title: A fall in AD on the Phillips curves
prompts.prompt: Starting at long-run equilibrium, AD in Varden falls. Explain the short-run effect on a correctly labeled graph of the Phillips curves.
checklist: Labels the axes: inflation rate and unemployment rate, with the LRPC vertical at the natural rate
Says the economy moves down along the SRPC (the curve does not shift)
Says unemployment rises above the natural rate and inflation falls

earns.answer: On the Phillips curve graph (inflation rate on the vertical axis, unemployment rate on the horizontal, LRPC vertical at the natural rate), a fall in AD moves the economy down along the SRPC to a new point. Unemployment rises above the natural rate and the inflation rate falls; neither curve shifts in the short run.
earns.why: Correct axes, a movement along the SRPC, and both outcomes compared with the start.

prompts.title: A supply shock on the Phillips curves
prompts.prompt: A sharp rise in energy prices hits firms across Varden. Explain the effect on the short-run Phillips curve and on inflation and unemployment.
checklist: Says SRAS shifts left in the AD-AS model
Says the SRPC shifts right (up)
Says inflation and unemployment both rise (stagflation)

earns.answer: Higher energy costs shift SRAS left, raising the price level faster while real output falls. On the Phillips curves this is a rightward shift of the SRPC: at each unemployment rate, inflation is higher. Both the inflation rate and the unemployment rate rise.
earns.why: It links the supply shock to the SRPC shift and states both outcomes.

misses.answer: The economy moves up along the SRPC: inflation rises and unemployment falls.
misses.why: That is the effect of more AD; a supply shock shifts the SRPC, and unemployment rises with inflation.

Firms produce less, so they employ fewer workers.

prompts.title: Back to the natural rate after a rise in AD
prompts.prompt: Varden's AD rises from long-run equilibrium, and unemployment falls below the natural rate. There is no policy response. Explain what happens in the long run, on the Phillips curves and in the AD-AS model.
checklist: Says workers come to expect the higher inflation and win higher nominal wages
Says SRAS shifts left in the AD-AS model, and the SRPC shifts right
Says unemployment returns to the natural rate at a higher inflation rate

earns.answer: The higher inflation comes to be expected, so workers bargain for higher nominal wages. Higher wage costs shift SRAS left in the AD-AS model, and on the Phillips curves the SRPC shifts right. Unemployment returns to the natural rate on the LRPC, but at a higher inflation rate than before.
earns.why: It names the cause (expected inflation and wages), the SRAS and SRPC shifts, and where the economy ends.

misses.answer: Unemployment stays low because inflation is higher.
misses.why: In the long run there is no trade-off; the answer has no expectations, no shift and no return to the natural rate.

Higher expected inflation raises inflation at each unemployment rate.
The LRPC is vertical: below the natural rate cannot last.

prompts.title: Money growth in the long run
prompts.prompt: Rellan's central bank raises the money supply by 10% a year for many years. Velocity is steady. Explain the long-run effect on real output and the price level, using the quantity theory of money.
checklist: Writes the equation of exchange, M x V = P x Y
Says real output in the long run is set by resources and technology, not money
Says faster money growth shows up as faster growth of the price level (inflation)

earns.answer: By M x V = P x Y, with V steady, faster growth of M means faster growth of P x Y. In the long run real output Y is set by resources and technology, not by money, so the extra money growth shows up as a faster rise in the price level P: inflation. Money is neutral in the long run.
earns.why: It uses the equation, says why output does not follow money, and draws the conclusion for prices.

misses.answer: More money lets people buy more, so real output grows faster.
misses.why: That can happen for a while in the short run; in the long run output depends on resources, so the extra money raises prices.

prompts.title: Computing velocity
prompts.prompt: In Rellan the money supply is 200 billion dollars, the price level is 2 and real output is 500 billion dollars. Calculate the velocity of money, and show your work.
checklist: Rearranges the equation to V = (P x Y) / M
Finds nominal GDP: 2 x 500 = 1,000 billion dollars
Gets V = 1,000 / 200 = 5 times a year

earns.answer: From M x V = P x Y, velocity is V = (P x Y) / M. Nominal GDP is 2 x 500 = 1,000 billion dollars, so V = 1,000 / 200 = 5: the average dollar is spent on final output 5 times a year.
earns.why: It rearranges the equation, computes nominal GDP, and divides, with every step shown.

prompts.title: A deficit and the national debt
prompts.prompt: Ostin's government collects 3,000 billion dollars in taxes and spends 3,400 billion dollars this year. Its national debt was 10,000 billion dollars at the start of the year. Calculate the budget balance and the debt at the end of the year.

Debt at the end = 10,000 + 400 = 10,400 billion dollars
Says a deficit is one year's shortfall while the debt is the total owed

earns.answer: The budget balance is revenue minus outlays: 3,000 - 3,400 = -400, a deficit of 400 billion dollars. The government borrows to cover it, so the debt rises to 10,000 + 400 = 10,400 billion dollars. The deficit is this year's shortfall; the debt is the total owed from all past deficits.
earns.why: Both numbers come with their steps, and the two ideas are kept apart.

prompts.title: From government borrowing to long-run growth

Says the real interest rate rises, so private investment falls (crowding out)
Says less investment means a smaller capital stock, so long-run growth is slower

earns.why: Every link from borrowing to growth is named, in order.

prompts.title: Growth on two graphs
prompts.prompt: Over a decade, workers in Pirro gain skills and firms adopt better technology. Explain how this shows on Pirro's PPC and on its LRAS curve.
checklist: Says the PPC shifts outward
Says LRAS shifts right, raising full-employment output
Names the causes: more human capital and better technology raise productivity

earns.answer: More skills (human capital) and better technology raise productivity, so the economy can produce more of everything. Its PPC shifts outward, and its LRAS curve shifts right, from LRAS1 to LRAS2, raising full-employment output: economic growth.
earns.why: Both graphs move the right way, and the causes are named.

prompts.title: A policy for growth, not for a recession
prompts.prompt: Pirro wants faster long-run growth in real GDP per person. Identify one policy that would most likely work and explain why a one-time rise in transfer payments would not.
checklist: Names a policy that adds capacity: tax credits for investment, spending on education or research
Says it raises physical or human capital or technology, shifting LRAS right
Says transfers raise AD for a while but add no capacity

earns.answer: Tax credits for business investment would add to physical capital, and spending on education would raise human capital; either raises productivity and shifts LRAS right, lifting real GDP per person over time. prompts.title: Where a transaction goes in the balance of payments
prompts.prompt: Identify where each is recorded in Arland's balance of payments: (1) an Arland firm sells machines to a buyer in Belvia; (2) an Arland resident buys bonds issued in Belvia.
checklist: (1) a credit in the current account (an export)
(2) a debit in the capital and financial account (buying a foreign asset)
Explains the rule: goods and services in the current account, assets in the capital and financial account

earns.answer: (1) Selling machines abroad is an export of goods, recorded as a credit in Arland's current account. (2) Buying Belvian bonds is a purchase of a foreign asset, an outflow recorded as a debit in Arland's capital and financial account. Trade in goods and services goes in the current account; trade in assets goes in the capital and financial account.
earns.why: Each entry is in the right account with the right sign, and the rule is stated.

prompts.title: The two accounts balance
prompts.prompt: Arland's current account has a deficit of 50 billion arls, and its central bank buys and sells no reserves. Calculate the balance of the capital and financial account, and explain why.
checklist: Says the two accounts sum to zero when the central bank does not trade reserves
Gets a capital and financial account surplus of 50 billion arls
Explains Arland pays for its extra imports by selling assets or borrowing from abroad

earns.answer: With no reserve transactions, the current account and the capital and financial account sum to zero, so the capital and financial account has a surplus of 50 billion arls: -50 + 50 = 0. Arland pays for buying more than it sells by selling assets to, or borrowing from, the rest of the world.
earns.why: It applies the balancing rule with the numbers and explains what the surplus means.

misses.answer: The capital and financial account also has a deficit of 50 billion arls.
misses.why: The two accounts offset each other; a current account deficit means a capital and financial account surplus.

The two sum to zero, so it is 50.
why.2: A deficit on one side means a surplus on the other.

prompts.title: Reading an exchange rate both ways
prompts.prompt: The exchange rate is 4 bels per arl. Calculate the price of one bel in arls, and the cost in arls of a Belvian bicycle priced at 100 bels.
checklist: One bel costs 1 / 4 = 0.25 arls
The bicycle costs 100 x 0.25 = 25 arls (or 100 / 4)
States the rate the right way round: bels per arl, so dividing by 4 turns bels into arls

earns.answer: If 1 arl buys 4 bels, one bel costs 1 / 4 = 0.25 arls. The bicycle costs 100 x 0.25 = 25 arls, the same as 100 / 4.
earns.why: Both prices are found with the rate used the right way round, and the work is shown.

misses.answer: The bicycle costs 100 x 4 = 400 arls in Arland's currency.
misses.why: That multiplies by bels per arl; to turn bels into arls divide by 4 (or multiply by 0.25 arls per bel).

why.1: 4 is bels per arl; flip it for arls per bel.
That multiplies bels by bels per arl.

prompts.title: Labeling the market for arls
prompts.prompt: Describe how to label a correctly drawn graph of the foreign exchange market for arls, and identify who demands and who supplies arls.
checklist: Vertical axis: the price of the arl in bels (bels per arl); horizontal axis: quantity of arls
Demand for arls comes from Belvians buying Arland goods, services and assets
Supply of arls comes from Arland residents buying Belvian goods, services and assets

earns.answer: The vertical axis is the price of the arl in the other currency, bels per arl, and the horizontal axis is the quantity of arls. Belvians who want Arland goods, services or assets demand arls; Arland residents who want Belvian goods, services or assets supply arls to get bels.
earns.why: The axis ratio is the right way round, and both sides of the market are named.

misses.answer: The vertical axis is arls per bel, and Arland residents demand arls.
misses.why: In the market for arls the price is bels per arl; and Arland residents supply arls when they buy abroad.

why.1: That is the price of the bel; in the market for arls, price the arl in bels.
Arland residents buying abroad need bels, so they supply arls.

prompts.title: The mirror market for bels
prompts.prompt: Belvians buy more Arland goods, so the demand for arls rises. Explain what happens in the market for bels at the same time.
checklist: Says Belvians supply bels to buy arls
Says the supply of bels shifts right
Says the bel depreciates, the mirror of the arl appreciating

earns.answer: To buy arls, Belvians offer bels, so the supply of bels shifts right in the market for bels. The price of the bel in arls falls: the bel depreciates. It is the mirror of the arl appreciating in the market for arls.
earns.why: It names the curve in the other market and its direction, and links it to the first market.

misses.answer: The demand for bels rises too, so both currencies appreciate.
misses.why: Two currencies cannot both appreciate against each other; Belvians supply bels to buy arls.

why.1: Belvians are giving up bels, so they supply them.
If the arl buys more bels, each bel buys fewer arls.

prompts.title: Higher incomes abroad and the arl
prompts.prompt: Incomes in Belvia rise, and Belvians buy more goods made in Arland. Explain the effect on the market for arls and on the value of the arl.
checklist: Says the demand for arls shifts right
Says the supply of arls does not change
Says the arl appreciates: its price in bels rises

earns.answer: Belvians need arls to buy Arland goods, so the demand for arls shifts right. Supply does not change, so the price of the arl in bels rises: the arl appreciates.
earns.why: The right curve moves the right way for the right reason, and the change in value is named.

misses.answer: The supply of arls rises, so the arl depreciates.
misses.why: Belvians buying Arland goods demand arls; nothing here makes Arland residents supply more.

why.1: Supply comes from Arland residents buying abroad, which did not change.
More demand raises the arl's price in bels.

prompts.title: A higher real interest rate and the arl
prompts.prompt: Arland's real interest rate rises relative to Belvia's. Explain the effect on the market for arls and on the value of the arl.
checklist: Says Belvian savers want more Arland assets
Says the demand for arls shifts right (and Arland residents supply fewer arls)
Says the arl appreciates: its price in bels rises

earns.answer: A higher real interest rate makes Arland's financial assets more attractive, so Belvian savers buy more of them and need arls to do it. The demand for arls shifts right (and Arland residents buy fewer Belvian assets, so they supply fewer arls), and the arl appreciates.
earns.why: It links the rate to asset purchases, names the curve, and gives the change in value.

misses.answer: The arl depreciates because Arland's interest rate is higher.
misses.why: A higher real rate draws foreign savers in, which raises the demand for the arl, so it appreciates.

why.1: Arland residents buying abroad supply arls, not demand them.
Higher demand for arls raises their price in bels.

prompts.title: From a stronger arl to aggregate demand
prompts.prompt: The arl appreciates against the bel. Explain the effect on Arland's net exports and aggregate demand, naming every link.
checklist: Says Arland goods cost more in bels, so Belvians buy fewer: exports fall
Says Belvian goods cost fewer arls, so Arland buys more: imports rise
Says net exports fall, so AD shifts left

earns.answer: A stronger arl makes Arland goods cost more in bels, so Belvians buy fewer of them and Arland's exports fall. It also makes Belvian goods cheaper in arls, so Arland imports rise. With exports down and imports up, net exports fall, which lowers aggregate demand, so AD shifts left.
earns.why: Every link from the exchange rate to AD is named, for both exports and imports.

misses.answer: The arl is stronger, so Arland's economy grows.
misses.why: A stronger currency lowers net exports, which lowers AD; the answer reverses the effect and skips every link.

why.1: Its goods now cost Belvians more bels.
Exports fall and imports rise, so net exports fall.
Lower net exports lower AD.

prompts.title: Lower rates, capital flows and net exports
prompts.prompt: Arland's central bank lowers its policy rate, lowering Arland's real interest rate. Explain the effect on capital flows, the value of the arl and Arland's net exports, naming every link.
checklist: Says lower real rates make Arland assets less attractive, so financial capital flows out
Says less demand for arls (and more supply) makes the arl depreciate
Says a weaker arl makes Arland exports cheaper abroad, so net exports rise

earns.answer: A lower real interest rate makes Arland's assets less attractive, so financial capital flows out of Arland. Belvians demand fewer arls and Arland residents supply more arls to buy Belvian assets, which makes the arl depreciate. A weaker arl makes Arland's exports cheaper in bels and imports dearer in arls, so Arland's net exports rise.
earns.why: Every link from the rate to net exports is named in order.

misses.answer: Lower rates make the arl weaker, so Arland exports more.
misses.why: The capital flow that links the rate to the arl is missing, and net exports (exports minus imports) are not named.

why.1: A lower real rate makes Arland's assets pay less, so savers move funds out.
Less demand and more supply of arls lower their price.
A weaker arl makes Arland's goods cheaper abroad.

prompts.title: The central bank's tool in an open economy
prompts.prompt: Arland, which has ample reserves, is in a recession. Identify the action its central bank would take and explain its effect on the arl.
checklist: Names lowering the interest rate on reserve balances (its administered rate)
Says the policy rate and Arland's interest rates fall
Says capital flows out and the arl depreciates, which raises net exports

earns.answer: The central bank lowers its administered rates, chiefly the interest rate on reserve balances, which lowers the policy rate and other Arland interest rates. Lower rates make Arland assets less attractive, so financial capital flows out and the arl depreciates, which raises net exports and adds to AD.
earns.why: The tool fits the framework and the problem, and its effect on the currency is linked through capital flows.

misses.answer: The central bank sells bonds to strengthen the arl.
misses.why: With ample reserves the tool is the administered rate, and a recession calls for lower rates, not tighter policy.

tool.label: The tool
options: lower the interest rate on reserve balances
raise the interest rate on reserve balances

why.1: Open market operations are the limited-reserves tool, and selling bonds is contractionary.
why.2: Raising rates would deepen the recession.

why.1: Lower Arland rates send capital out, lowering the demand for arls.

prompts.title: Labeling a graph from a table
prompts.context:
A teacher records hours studied and test scores.

Hours studied1234
Test score (points)60708085
prompts.prompt: Describe how to label a graph of these data, and identify the point for a student who studies 3 hours.
checklist: Puts hours studied on the horizontal axis and the test score on the vertical axis, each with its units
Names the point (3, 80) as hours first, then score
Says the graph shows a direct relationship: more hours, a higher score

earns.answer: Hours studied goes on the horizontal axis (hours) and the test score on the vertical axis (points). The student who studies 3 hours is the point (3, 80): 3 across, then up to 80. The scores rise as hours rise, so the graph shows a direct relationship.
earns.why: Both axes are named with their units, the point is read in the right order, and the relationship is named.

misses.answer: Put the numbers on the graph and plot the point 80, 3.
misses.why: No axis is named, and the point is written with the score first, so it lands in the wrong place.

why.1: The score depends on the hours, so the hours go across and the score goes up.
A point is written across first, then up: (hours, score).

rel.label: The relationship
options: inverse: one rises as the other falls

why.1: The score rises when hours rise, which is a direct relationship.

prompts.title: The slope between two points
prompts.context:
A piano student's practice hours and recital score:

Practice (hours)24
Score (points)5070
prompts.prompt: Calculate the slope of the line from 2 hours to 4 hours on the graph of these data, and explain what it means.
checklist: Writes rise over run with the two points: (70 - 50) divided by (4 - 2)
Gets 10 points per hour, with the units
Says each extra hour of practice adds about 10 points on this part of the graph

earns.answer: The slope is the rise over the run: (70 - 50) / (4 - 2) = 20 / 2 = 10 points per hour. Each extra hour of practice between 2 and 4 hours adds about 10 points to the score.
earns.why: The rise and the run come from the two points, the answer has its units, and the meaning is stated.

misses.answer: The slope is 20, because the score goes up by 20.
misses.why: That is the rise alone; the slope divides it by the run, 2 hours, and gives no units.

why.1: Slope is rise over run: the change in the vertical variable goes on top.
20 is the rise; divide by the run of 2 hours.
why.2: That is run over rise; flip it.

prompts.title: A movement along a curve or a shift
prompts.prompt: A graph shows a runner's heart rate against her running speed. Explain whether each change moves her along the curve or shifts the whole curve: (1) she runs faster; (2) after months of training, her heart rate is lower at every speed.
checklist: Says a change in the variable on an axis (speed) is a movement along the curve
Says a change in something not on the axes (fitness) shifts the whole curve
States the direction of the shift: down, a lower heart rate at each speed

earns.answer: (1) Speed is on the horizontal axis, so running faster is a movement along the curve to a higher heart rate. (2) Fitness is not on either axis, so training shifts the whole curve: it moves down, because her heart rate is lower at every speed.
earns.why: It tells the two cases apart by whether the change is on an axis, and it gives the direction of the shift.

misses.answer: Both shift the curve, because her heart rate changes.
misses.why: A change in heart rate alone does not say which; only a factor off the axes shifts the curve, and the direction is missing.

why.1: Speed is on an axis, so a change in it moves along the curve.
Fitness is not on an axis, so it shifts the curve.
why.2: Her heart rate is lower at every speed, so the curve moves down.

prompts.title: Before and after a crossing point moves
prompts.prompt: Two lines cross at point E1. One line shifts right, and they now cross at E2, up and to the right of E1. Describe the change on both axes and how to show it on the graph.
checklist: Compares E2 with E1 on the horizontal axis: higher
Compares E2 with E1 on the vertical axis: higher
Labels the new line and the new crossing point, with dashed lines to both axes

earns.answer: E2 is to the right of E1, so the value on the horizontal axis is higher, and E2 is above E1, so the value on the vertical axis is higher too. On the graph, label the shifted line with a 2, mark E2 where the lines now cross, and draw dashed lines from E1 and E2 to both axes so the two values can be compared.
earns.why: Both axes are compared before and after, and the graph shows the new line and point clearly.

misses.answer: The crossing point moved, so both lines changed.
misses.why: Only one line shifted; and the answer never says which way each value changed.

why.1: E2 is to the right of E1, so the horizontal value is higher.
why.2: E2 is not straight above E1; it moved right.

why.1: E2 is above E1, so the vertical value is higher.
